query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: For AlCrFeNiSi miniature components, using in‐situ substrate preheating at approximately 400°C combined with real-time laser power modulation during SLM will reduce residual thermal stresses and improve the mechanical properties relative to conventional high-thermal-load processing.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock with typical particle size distribution and purity for SLM processing.
generation.intervention: Implement in‐situ substrate preheating at ~400°C under an inert atmosphere during SLM, paired with real-time laser power modulation.
generation.conditions: Processing performed in an SLM system within a substrate preheating temperature window of 200°C to 600°C (optimized near 400°C) under an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon with low oxygen levels). Tests are conducted on miniature component geometries, with residual stresses measured via X-ray diffraction and mechanical properties evaluated through nanoindentation and microhardness testing.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction of thermal gradients during layer deposition leads to a more uniform, fine-grained microstructure with lower internal stresses.
generation.mechanism: Preheating minimizes steep thermal gradients and rapid cooling, thereby reducing contraction-induced residual stresses while real-time laser power modulation ensures optimized energy deposition. This coordinated thermal management moderates the solidification process to yield reduced defect formation and improved mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The intervention is expected to produce miniature components with significantly lower residual thermal stresses and enhanced mechanical properties (e.g., increased hardness and more uniform microstructure) compared to components fabricated under conventional high-thermal-load SLM conditions.
generation.baseline: Components processed without substrate preheating, where rapid cooling leads to high thermal gradients, increased residual stresses, and degraded mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to SLM-fabricated miniature components of AlCrFeNiSi under controlled inert atmospheres with substrate preheating between 200°C and 600°C; results might differ with other component sizes, geometries, or alloy systems.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements and the optimum preheating temperature require further detailed experimentation; additional factors such as powder variations or machine-specific parameters may influence outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two groups of miniature AlCrFeNiSi components via SLM: one using standard conditions (no substrate preheating) and one using the proposed in‐situ substrate preheating at 400°C with real-time laser power modulation. Ensure all other processing parameters are consistent.
measurements: Residual stress analysis using X-ray diffraction
Mechanical testing via nanoindentation and microhardness measurements
Defect analysis (e.g., hot crack detection) and density measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the components fabricated with in‐situ substrate preheating do not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical properties and a reduction in residual thermal stresses, relative to the standard processing group, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The Ni35Co35Cr25Ti3Al2 MEA was additively manufactured using a SLM280HL (SLM Solutions, Germany) LPBF machine equipped with a maximum power of 400 W fiber laser (spot diameter: 80 µm). Rectangular blocks with dimensions of 60 × 15 × 15 mm3 were built on a 316 L stainless steel substrate. To minimize thermal residual stresses, the build plate was pre-heated to 200 °C and maintained at this temperature throughout the process. The optimized processing parameters employed were: laser power = 320 W, scanning velocity = 1000 mm/s, hatch distance = 0.07 mm, and layer thickness = 0.03 mm, resulting in a volume energy density of about 152 J/mm3 and samples with >99.6% density. A 67° rotational scan strategy was used. The deposition process was carried out under an inert argon atmosphere with oxygen concentration below 300 ppm to minimize oxidation. After the LPBF process, the built samples were cut off from the build plate via electro-discharge machining (EDM).

Eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) exhibit excellent casting properties and comprehensive mechanical performance, making them suitable for fabricating spatial engineering components using additive manufacturing techniques. However, the rapid solidification process also leads to increased internal stress and reduced structural stability in the components. Therefore, this study focuses on the AlFeCoCrNi2.1 EHEA as the research subject, utilizing laser additive manufacturing to fabricate components and systematically investigating the influence of heat treatment processes on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the components. The research demonstrates that low-temperature heat treatment (700 °C and below) acts as a stress relief-annealing process for the components. The yield strength decreased from 1003.2 MPa to 742.1 MPa. At 900 °C heat treatment, the constraining effect between recrystallized grains and surrounding grains outweighs the dislocation release effect caused by recrystallization, resulting in an increase in dislocation density. AbstractHigh-entropy alloys are known for their promising mechanical properties, wear and corrosion resistance, which are maintained across a wide range of temperatures. In this study, a CoCrFeNiCu-based high-entropy alloy, distinguished from conventional CoCrFeNi systems by the addition of Cu, which is known to enhance toughness and wear resistance, was investigated to better understand the effects of compositional modification on processability and performance. The influence of key process parameters, specifically laser power and scan speed, on the processability of CoCrFeNiCu-based high-entropy alloys produced by laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing was investigated, with a focus of low laser power, which is critical for minimizing defects and improving the resulting microstructure and mechanical performance. The printed sample density gradually increases with higher volumetric energy density, achieving densities exceeding 99.0%. However, at higher energy densities, the samples exhibit susceptibility to hot cracking, an issue that cannot be mitigated by adjusting the process parameters. chosen.technique: selective laser melting using real‐time laser power modulation combined with controlled substrate heating

chosen.why: This move directly fills the open niche by replacing conventional high‐thermal-load regimes with controlled thermal management. By leveraging established preheating techniques in selective laser melting, it systematically reduces thermal gradients and residual stresses, thereby alleviating degradation in mechanical properties and simplifying processing—making it a plausible, targeted intervention given the state‐of‐the‐art in metallic additive manufacturing.
